title: THE BOY AND THE HERON & THE KILLER

commenti.body:
I mean, you can’t separate your reaction to a film from its context, which includes your personal context. Which is what makes art so amazing, as the sum total of the experience of art is the coming together of the artist’s intent and decision making, and your personal experience, biases, etc.

So I don’t think there’s anything wrong with enjoying one film whilst criticising another for the same reasons. One resonated with you, one didn’t.

Also, if I may weigh in on these two films in particular, The Boy and the Heron purports to be “about” big things in life… life, death, grief, etc. Wheras The Killer is very much a film almost about movies themselves, and very much wedded to a specific genre and commenting on/satirising that.

So if Miyazaki falls short, that’s because his ambition with the story wasn’t really matched with the payoff and execution, whereas I think Fincher’s aims are perhaps less “ambitious” from a story and emotional point of view, but he nails it in my opinion, and then some.

Thank you for replying! 

I guess i was so caught up because my personal experience was impacted by my personal effort in knowing so much about a director versus the other. If I didn’t know so much about Fincher, would I even have liked the film as much as I did? Would I have liked The Boy and the Heron more if I knew more about Miyazaki? I didn’t make the connection between Ghibli failing to find an heir and the great uncle with Mahito, and what that would do to this world he spent a lifetime building and maintaining. And that’s just 1 insight provided by a little bit of context of Miyazaki’s life. 

I think the answer lies in me taking the time to learn more and go do a rewatch, but i was hoping it could create some discussion.

Without spoilers, can you elaborate on how The Killer is Fincher commentating on his own career and repuation?  
  
I think KOTFM had the same effect with Scorsese, especially with the ending. It's more poignant knowing his career; same with The Irishman.

I definitely agree with your insight about the intimate weaving of a director's personal narrative within their filmic work. It adds extra dimensions for the keen-eyed audience to discover. However, I think it's not quite hypocritical to commend Fincher's 'The Killer' while critiquing Miyazaki's 'The Boy and the Heron'. The latter might not have struck the right chord with you due to its execution or it simply lacked the classic Miyazaki charm that resonates with his fans.

Your point about fairness for a director to expect the audience to be well-acquainted with their personal life is compelling. A fine balance needs to be struck here. While filmmakers often channel their personal stories, a film should be able to withstand scrutiny on its own, without the audience needing to delve deep into the director's life for appreciation. However, when the echelons of a director's life become apparent through deeper scrutiny, the viewing experience can be elevated.

One plausible angle is that 'The Boy and the Heron' leaned a bit too heavily on insider knowledge about Miyazaki compared to Fincher's 'The Killer'. The former might have slipped slightly in the execution of this subtlety.

At the core, I believe filmmakers craft their narratives aiming at the audience. Despite infusing personal anecdotes or social commentary, the film's quality largely depends on how seamlessly these personal elements are integrated into the plot. To address your last query, I feel digging deeper and understanding the backstory can transform a film from being mundane to fascinating, sparking endless debates and interpretations, which to me, is the essence of our shared love for cinema.

Thank you for your well-crafted reply! I really appreciate you deciding to engage with this post.   


I particularly enjoyed how you phrased the following:

>However, when the echelons of a director's life become apparent through deeper scrutiny, the viewing experience can be elevated.

I think I ultimately agree with this sentiment. a film should be enhanced, not dependent on, this understanding.

I think that while there is a lot of Miyazaki in The Boy and the Heron, it also works without that context.

A young boy violently loses his mother and is clearly still dwelling on it to his own detriment. He ends up going on a fantastical adventure where he gets to see his mother one last time, while also learning to accept his new mother as part of his family. Even when given the chance to live in a paradise of his own making, he chooses to return to the real world because he’s finally grown enough to move on with his life.

That doesn’t explain every single detail, but that’s a fairly surface level reading of the film that doesn’t rely on any knowledge of Miyazaki’s life or work.

I will try my best.

​

The Killer is basically David Fincher himself as a director, and the film lightly pokes fun at his reputation. He is a precise shooter, extremely meticulous, and has an intense work ethic. The titular Killer goes to impressive but almost psychotic lengths to prepare for his job, and maybe that alone is a commentary on the type of person that would become a director in the first place lol. 

The joke is that no matter how much you prepare and how seriously you take this job, there is only so much you can control. Many people have shared their reading of the film being about some guy that is not as good as he thinks he is. I refute that completely.  I think it is about a guy that is extremely good at his job, makes a mistake, hates feeling out of control, is so passionate about his job that it is sacred for him, and takes the necessary lengths to make the necessary adjustments to retain his control. I also think its about a guy who cant help but to do his job. 

I will add one spoilery comment to further solidify my point: >!in the film, the Killer confronts multiple targets of his. these targets end up being so shaken by his prescence and their fate that they end up rambling on and on. The Killer never engages in conversation with them, and rarely speaks at all. I think this is indicative of Fincher and his works, especially Fight Club, Seven, Benjamin Button, The Social Network, and now The Killer. His works are more like litmus tests that say more about the audience than Fincher himself, and I think Fincher prefers it that way. He does not really care to engage with what you take away from the film or if you think hes a bad person for making it. He is just focused on killing it, doing the job right, so he can go do the next one. !<

I don’t think it’s a directors job to appeal to his Audience. He’s an artist who used his art to express his self in a deeply personal way for the purpose of - by his own words - saying (to his grandson) “Grandpa is moving onto the next world soon but he is leaving behind this film”.  That’s about as pure as art gets- I’m glad we get to experience it. Now, I don’t think one has to know about Miyazaki to appreciate the coming of age themes the movies presents throughout. Mahito is presented with a broken and cruel world and chooses throughout the film to use his little part in it to be good to others. There’s a culminating passage in the novel Miyazaki was inspired by “How Do You Live” that stated (spoilers of the book if you care) 

“I think there has to come a time when every one in the world treats each other as if they were good friends. Since humanity has come so far, I think now we will definitely be able to make it to such a place.” So I think I want to become a person who can help that happen.” 

I think it’s this philosophy that Mahito adopts after reading the book in the film- and what you see on his journey is the young boy learning what it means to live this philosophy. From this, if you watch this movie with the eyes of a teen (who will accept the convoluted rules of the fantasy world without question, because the real world is just as enigmatic to a boy) then I find it can be simply appreciated for what it is. All the deep layers of Miyazakis self are still there and ripe for reflection- but the movie stands on its own as a moralistic fantasy adventure.

Makes you wonder if there is something corresponding in his own career that Fincher considers a "mistake".

He seems bummed out by how expensive and ambitious Mindhunters became with no real pay off.

i disagree that he is good to others. he is really a blank slate. if anything, he is a very respectful young boy who is obviously dealing with a lot internally due to what he has been through, but hes not really fleshed out and i dont really see any examples of him being "good". He isnt "bad" either, and thats my point about the film. You can see crumbs of something Miyazaki is trying to do, and some audiences have filled in the spaces but i dont think that is enough. 

The boy doesnt ever state he doesnt accept his position. He never states he doesnt like his mom. He doesnt ever suggest anything really except that he knows that heron is pestering him. So there isnt even really any growth. He calls his new mother "mom", but he never seemed to resist doing so either. He just keeps going through this story until its over.

being cut off from finishing it probably really fucks with a guy like Fincher for sure, but also it could be Alien3, or Dragon Tattoo because that was supposed to be a franchise he was going to build, or Mank because many people talked it down and still do to this day and its clear that it was a personal project due to his father writing the script before he passed.   


And funnily enough, it can also be about how a he can be a super prepared director but if it the weather does not cooperate and youre rained out, then there was nothing you COULD do about it and there isnt anything you CAN do about it. It is time to improvise and adjust. And maybe the other joke is that when Fincher improvises and adjusts, he is just as meticulous with that, only to be shit on by the fickle and volatile nature of filmmaking.

Going to save Nasuke, Helping get the boat out to sea, helping with cutting the fish, digging the grave, fixing the hole in the heron so he can fly (even after the pelican betrays him), etc. the film is full of little moments where Mahito chooses to be helpful. He’s a subtle character- but I disagree he’s a blank slate.
